title: En Tibi herbarium, leaf with a tomato specimen labelled "Poma Amoris"
summary: A single leaf of the En Tibi herbarium, a bound Renaissance herbarium assembled in Italy in 1542-1544 and now held by the Naturalis Biodiversity Center, Leiden. The leaf carries three pressed and mounted specimens, numbered 292, 293 and 294 in a contemporary hand. Specimen 294, at the upper right, is a tomato: pinnately compound leaves with irregularly lobed leaflets, and one dried fruit still attached to its stalk. The label at the foot of its stem reads "Poma Amoris" -- the love-apple name this corpus already tracks for Solanum lycopersicum, and the same term that makes Covarrubias 1611 the corpus's calibration case for a false positive, since there it denotes the aubergine. Naturalis identifies the specimen as Solanum lycopersicum var. lycopersicum and describes it as one of the oldest conserved tomato specimens in Europe, the second oldest known. The evidence here is the physical plant itself and the name written beside it: this is a specimen, not a text about a specimen.

author: Charles de l'Écluse (Clusius)
summary: One volume of the Libri picturati, the largest surviving collection of Renaissance plant watercolours, made in the Low Countries in the second half of the sixteenth century and now at the Biblioteka Jagiellońska in Kraków as Libri picturati A 28. The Jagiellonian's own title for the volume is "Des toutes sortes des racines, fleurs et fruicts". It matters here for one leaf: the digitisation's image 120 is a life-size watercolour of a tomato truss — three ripe fruits in deep red and three unripe in green, every one of them strongly flattened and deeply ribbed, hanging from thick cut stems, with the calyx drawn on each and a ghost of tomato foliage showing through from the facing leaf. It is a painted observation of a ribbed tomato from within a generation or two of the plant's arrival in Europe, and it is drawn from life rather than copied from an earlier herbal block.

title: Cruijdeboeck — "Van Gulden appelen", the tomato chapter and woodcut, folio 471
author: Rembert Dodoens
summary: The tomato chapter of Rembert Dodoens's Cruijdeboeck (Antwerp, van der Loe, 1554), folio 471. The hand-coloured woodcut is captioned in two languages at once — "Poma amoris." on the left and "Gulden appelen." on the right — and shows a branching plant with pinnate lobed leaves, yellow star-shaped flowers and small red fruits in clusters, round to slightly flattened rather than ribbed. Dodoens opens the chapter by dividing the fruit into two kinds: "Dese vremde appelen sijn oock tweederleye / die eene sijn root / die andere bleeck geel / anders van stelen / bladeren ende wasse in alle manieren malcanderen ghelijckende" — these foreign apples are of two sorts, one red, the other pale yellow, alike in stems, leaves and growth in every other way. The chapter ending at the head of the same page is the aubergine, under Mala insana, Verangenes, Melantzan and Dulle appel. The copy is the Rijksmuseum's, hand-coloured by Hans Liefrinck (1520-1573). The book's hand-coloured title page is held beside this leaf as a page scan, not as a work of its own: it carries no tomato.

title: De hortis Germaniae liber — the "Pomum aureum uel amoris" entry, folio 273r
author: Conrad Gessner
summary: Conrad Gessner's garden book of 1561, at the entry "Pomum aureum uel amoris dictum" — the golden apple, or love apple. Gessner describes a foreign summer shrub akin to the nightshades, and adds the caution that gives the entry its weight: "Solanum pomiferum dixeris, sed alterum, ad Mali insani differentiam" — you would call it Solanum pomiferum, but a different one, to be distinguished from the aubergine. He says the fruit is nearly scentless, neither unpleasant nor harmful as food, the size of a small round apple, often larger, "inaequalis & tuberosus" — uneven and lumpy — and that it comes in THREE colours: golden, in a second sort red, in a third white. He records growing it successfully in Germany, in beds or pots, with watering and rich soil. He closes by noting that some people call the aubergine Pomum amoris too. The work was printed at Strasbourg by Josias Rihel in 1561 as part of the volume containing Valerius Cordus's Annotationes in Dioscoridem, which this corpus holds in full as a separate work.

title: Avrea mala — the tomato woodcut, Dodoens 1583, printed page 455
author: Rembertus Dodonaeus
summary: The tomato woodcut from Dodoens's Stirpium historiae pemptades sex (Antwerp, Plantin, 1583), printed page 455, captioned on the block "Aurea mala." and illustrating chapter XXX, "De aureis Malis". The plant is drawn whole, root to tip, with pinnate irregularly cut leaves and fruits borne in clusters — round and deeply ribbed, lobed into segments like a small pumpkin. That is precisely what the chapter says in words beside it: "fructus rotundi, profundis crenis striati", round fruits furrowed with deep notches, ripening "aut pulchre rubentes, aut auri luteo relucentes colore", either beautifully red or shining golden-yellow. The chapter also gives the plant's names in four languages at once — Itali Pomi d'oro, Germani Goltopffel, Belgae Gulden appel, Galli Pomme d'amours, id est Amoris poma.

title: Stirpium historiae pemptades sex — "De aureis Malis" (cap. XXX), the tomato chapter, printed pages 454-455
author: Rembertus Dodonaeus
summary: Two leaves of Dodoens's Stirpium historiae pemptades sex (Antwerp, Plantin, 1583), printed pages 454 and 455, carrying the tomato chapter "De aureis Malis", cap. XXX. Page 455 sets two woodcuts one above the other: AVREA MALA, a tomato plant whose fruits are drawn round and deeply ribbed, and MALA INSANA, the aubergine — the two plants the corpus keeps finding conflated, pictured on one page. Dodoens gives the tomato's names across four languages in a single line, records that it is sown in gardens and fruits the same year in autumn, notes it is eaten cooked with pepper, salt and oil, and separates it explicitly from the mythological golden apples of the Hesperides. Two chapters later, at cap. XXXI, he gives the AUBERGINE the French name "Pommes d'amours" as well.

title: Insect, Moth Mullein, Forget-Me-Not, and Tomato (Mira calligraphiae monumenta, fol. 42)
author: Joris Hoefnagel (illuminator); Georg Bocskay (scribe)
summary: A leaf of the Mira calligraphiae monumenta, the Habsburg model book of calligraphy: Georg Bocskay wrote the script in 1561-1562 for Ferdinand I, and about thirty years later Rudolf II had Joris Hoefnagel illuminate the finished book. Hoefnagel's illumination on this leaf shows a moth mullein, a spray of water forget-me-not, a fly, and one large tomato lying detached on the vellum. The fruit is markedly OBLATE and STRONGLY RIBBED into roughly ten lobes, with a dried recurved calyx in a shallow depression, and is caught RIPENING -- green-yellow over most of the body, flushing orange and red on one shoulder. Its companion leaf fol. 102 shows the same morphotype fully ripe and red. The tomato is Hoefnagel's work, so it is evidence for 1591-1596 and not for the 1561 script.

title: Martagon Lily and Tomato (Mira calligraphiae monumenta, fol. 102)

title: Archetypa studiaque patris Georgii Hoefnagelii, Pars IV, plate 9 ('Forma breuis flos est primo spectabilis ortu')
author: Jacob Hoefnagel (engraver), after Joris Hoefnagel
summary: One plate of the Archetypa studiaque, the engraved series Jacob Hoefnagel published in 1592 after his father Joris Hoefnagel's nature studies. The sheet arranges a pear, snails, a slug, a woodlouse, caterpillars, a garden spider, a crane fly, a moth, a bee, a carnation, jasmine and a white narcissus-like flower round two Latin mottoes -- and, top centre, ONE TOMATO: oblate, deeply lobed into about eight rounded segments, with a dried brown star-shaped calyx and a stem stub in a shallow sunken well, hand-coloured orange-red. The morphology agrees closely with the tomato on Getty Ms. 20 fol. 102, acquired in the same batch, without copying it: the angle, lobe count and colour differ. Two media from one workshop within five years, and this one was PRINTED -- multiplied and circulated rather than shut in an imperial manuscript.

title: Poma amoris fructu luteo — the yellow tomato, Hortus Eystettensis (1613), Bildtafel 319
author: Basilius Besler
summary: A hand-coloured copper engraving from the autumn order of Basilius Besler's Hortus Eystettensis (1613), carrying three plants of which the centre one is a tomato. The engraved captions read, left to right as printed: "II. Melo Saccharinus variegatus", "I Poma amoris fructu luteo.", "III. Pseudocolocynthis Pomiformis." The tomato is number I: a branching plant with pinnate irregularly lobed leaves, star-shaped pale flowers, and pale yellow to cream fruits drawn strongly ribbed and markedly flattened. Besler's own printed index lists it at Fol. 1 and the 1640 edition glosses it in German as "Lieböpffel oder Goldöpffel". Together with Bildtafel 320, the red-fruited kind, it shows Besler treating the two fruit colours as separate named kinds in 1613.

title: Poma amoris fructu rubro — the red tomato, Hortus Eystettensis (1613), Bildtafel 320
author: Basilius Besler
summary: A hand-coloured copper engraving of a red tomato plant, filling a whole plate of the autumn order of Basilius Besler's Hortus Eystettensis (1613). The engraved caption at the foot reads "Poma amoris fructu rubro." — love-apple with red fruit. The plant carries eight or more large fruits, deep red, heavily ribbed and strongly flattened, together with several smaller unripe green and brown fruits, star-shaped pale flowers, and pinnate irregularly lobed leaves; the artist's monogram is engraved at the base of the stem. Besler's own printed index to the Classis Autumnalis lists it at Fol. 2 and the 1640 edition glosses it in German as "Rothe Goldöpffel / Lieböpffel". This is the plate a rare-book dealer's listing described, which was all the corpus held for Besler until 2026-09-03.

title: Hortus Eystettensis (1613), Ordo Autumnalis — Besler's printed index and the tomato plate captions
author: Basilius Besler
summary: Two plates from the autumn order of Basilius Besler's Hortus Eystettensis, the great folio florilegium of the bishop's garden at Eichstätt, published in 1613. Besler figures the tomato TWICE, as two named kinds distinguished by fruit colour: Bildtafel 319 captions the centre plant "Poma amoris fructu luteo" — love-apple with yellow fruit — beside a striped sugar melon and a false colocynth; Bildtafel 320 gives a whole plate to "Poma amoris fructu rubro", the red-fruited kind. In both, the fruit is drawn heavily ribbed and strongly flattened, and the plant carries star-shaped pale flowers on pinnate lobed leaves. The 1640 edition glosses the two in German as "Lieböpffel oder Goldöpffel" and "Rothe Goldöpffel / Lieböpffel", tying the Latin poma amoris directly to the German love-apple and gold-apple names. These are the images themselves, from the coloured Fürstenausgabe held at Eichstätt as KU 2894; the corpus previously carried only a rare-book dealer's description of the 1640 red plate.

title: Hortulus Monheimensis — "Gartenblume Goldapfel (Tomatenpflanze)", fol. 144r
summary: A leaf of the Hortulus Monheimensis, a manuscript florilegium made in southern Germany in 1615 and held by the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek as Cod.icon. 31. Folio 144r is captioned, in the manuscript's own German, "Gartenblume Goldapfel (Tomatenpflanze)" — garden flower, gold apple, tomato plant. The Goldapfel name is the German counterpart of the Italian pomodoro and the Latin mala aurea that the corpus tracks elsewhere, and this is an early-seventeenth-century German instance of it applied to a painted plant.

title: Tomate Trentham Earlij Fillbasket -- a bunch of tomatoes (Lycopersicon esculentum), chromolithograph
author: Pierre Joseph de Pannemaeker
summary: A Belgian chromolithograph of a single truss of eight or nine tomatoes, captioned on the sheet 'Tomate Trentham Earlij Fillbasket' -- a named English cultivar. The fruit is ROUND to barely oblate, ESSENTIALLY UNRIBBED, uniform in size across the whole truss, deep crimson when ripe; two fruits are shown unripe with large leafy green calyces of long recurved sepals, and the background carries outline drawings of the pinnate tomato foliage. A chromolithograph exists to sell a variety, so what it shows is what a seedsman wanted a buyer to want: smoothness and uniformity. Set beside the two Hoefnagel tomatoes of 1591-1596 acquired in the same batch -- large, flat, deeply lobed -- it is the other end of the corpus's argument about 19th-century breeding.
